title: A Scene You Can Leave: A Five-Minute Guided-Imagery Practice
subtitle: A short, optional exercise in imagining a place, object or sensory detail—without needing vivid pictures, controlled breathing or a particular result.
imageAlt: Two friends sit comfortably at a kitchen table, one reading a short prompt while the other looks toward a sunlit window.
imageConcept: Two friends sharing a quiet pause at a kitchen table: one has a small card with a gentle imagery prompt, while the other sits with eyes open, grounded in the familiar room.
body:
Guided imagery can sound like a demand to picture a beach, feel instantly calm and report back that it worked. That version leaves little room for people who do not see clear mental pictures, who find certain scenes uncomfortable, or who simply do not want to turn a quiet moment into a performance. A more humane approach treats imagery as an invitation: choose a scene or object, notice whatever comes to mind, and stop when you want.

The practice below takes about five minutes, but the time is a boundary, not a target to endure. It does not require closing your eyes, regulating your breathing or sharing private thoughts. A remembered corner of a garden, an imagined room, a mug on a table—or only a word such as “shade”—can be enough. Nothing needs to be picturesque. The point is to make a little room for attention, not to produce a prescribed feeling.

The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs describes guided imagery as bringing positive images to mind, with the practice possible through a professional, a recording or self-guidance after learning the skill. Its overview discusses use in care settings and research evidence; it does not establish that an informal five-minute exercise will help everyone [1]. That distinction matters. A personal practice can be worth trying without being treated as a treatment or a guaranteed route to relaxation.

Research cited in the field also studies specific formats and groups, not every version of a brief exercise. In one randomized experiment, 40 community adults were assigned to either nature-based guided imagery or nature-based meditation, using audio sessions of about 20 minutes over two weeks. The researchers described their findings as preliminary and called for larger studies and clinical samples [3]. Those results do not test this five-minute practice, and they are not a promise about how any one person will feel.

So the useful question is modest: does this particular exercise feel acceptable to try, and is it easy to stop? If the answer is no, skipping it is a sound choice.
Start with the room you’re in

Choose a place where you can comfortably pause and give the practice your attention. Do not try it while driving, crossing a street or doing anything that needs focus. Sit, stand or recline in a way that works for your body. Keep your eyes open, lower your gaze or close them; there is no preferred setting. First notice one ordinary point of contact: feet on the floor, a hand on a table, or your back against a chair.

This brief orientation helps keep the actual room in view as the starting point and the destination. It is not a test of mindfulness, and you do not have to make your body feel different. If you would rather stay with the real surroundings than imagine anything, look at an object nearby and notice its color or outline. That is a complete version of the exercise.
Choose a scene with a clear exit

Pick something neutral or pleasant that feels manageable today. It might be a place you remember, a setting you invent, a familiar object, or a simple sensory quality such as cool shade. You do not need to choose the “best” memory or the place you think you ought to find soothing. If choosing a scene feels difficult, use an ordinary object instead: a bowl, a coat sleeve, a leaf or a patch of light.

Let one or two details arrive without trying to build a perfect picture. Perhaps there is a color, the suggestion of a sound, a sense of warmth or coolness, a texture, or just a word. Imagery can involve senses beyond sight, including sound, temperature and touch; it need not be visually vivid [2]. Some people may notice no sensory detail at all. You can stay with the object’s name or the idea of the scene rather than forcing a picture into focus.
A five-minute version, step by step

Set a timer if knowing when the exercise ends would help; otherwise, keep the duration loose. For the first minute, settle and notice the chair, floor or room. For the next minute, choose your scene or object. For a minute or two, gently attend to one or two details—or to the words you have chosen. If your attention wanders, there is no need to correct it. You can return to the detail, change it, or decide you have had enough.

Then pause. Ask yourself only whether you want to continue. If yes, stay with the scene briefly; if no, let it go. To finish, notice the real room again: the light, the shape of the furniture, your feet or hands against a surface. You might name one thing you can see. The ending is a return to ordinary surroundings, not a judgment about whether you relaxed.

This structure is a practical suggestion, not a tested protocol. Studies of other guided-imagery sessions have used longer, structured formats, so their findings should not be casually transferred to this shorter, self-led version [3].
Make stopping part of the practice

A remembered or imagined scene will not feel comfortable for everyone, every time. If an image becomes upsetting, confusing or too intense, stop rather than trying to push through. Open your eyes if they are closed, look around the room, name a few things you see, and feel the support beneath your feet or hands. You can also switch to noticing a real object or end the exercise altogether.

The VA’s Whole Health Library notes that self-guided imagery may not be appropriate in some circumstances, including unprocessed trauma, psychosis or difficulty distinguishing fantasy from reality [2]. This is a reason for care, not a diagnosis. If you have concerns about whether imagery is suitable for you, speak with a qualified health professional rather than treating a solo exercise as a substitute for support. Opting out is not failure; it is useful information about what feels right now.

Two friends can try the practice side by side, but neither needs to act as a therapist or explain what the other person’s scene means. Ask first whether the person wants to try it. One friend can read a short prompt—“Notice the room; choose a place or object; see what detail, if any, comes to mind; stop whenever you like”—then leave quiet space. The listener can keep their eyes open, change the prompt or stop without explaining why.

When the pause ends, let the person decide whether to say anything. “Would you like to tell me how that was, or leave it there?” makes room for both answers. If the scene felt uncomfortable, the helpful response is not to investigate it or insist that the person reimagine it more positively. Return to the present room, offer ordinary company and respect the boundary. The practice is private even when it is shared.
Let the scene end on your terms

For a first try, choose a moment when you are not rushing and a place where you can comfortably pause. Decide in advance that you can keep your eyes open, switch from a scene to an object, or stop at any point. Begin with the real room. Let one detail—or only a word—stand in for the imagined setting, and give it a minute or two without trying to make it vivid. Then look around again and notice your feet, hands or the surface supporting you. If another person is there, they can offer the prompt and keep the silence; they do not need to hear what you imagined. End with whatever feels complete, including no scene at all.
